Hasina seeks passport to return, govt insists on extradition
item.description:
Former prime minister Sheikh Hasina has formally sought a new Bangladeshi passport and national identity card to facilitate her planned return from India in December, but the government on Monday made clear that it wants her brought back through the extradition treaty rather than allowing her to return as a traveller.
The development, first reported by Reuters, marks Hasina’s first known formal communication with Bangladeshi authorities since she left for India following the mass uprising in August 2024.
While State Minister for Foreign Affairs Humaiun Kobir dismissed the application and insisted on extradition, Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed said the government was examining its authenticity, legal basis and procedural validity.
The International Crimes Tribunal’s chief prosecutor, meanwhile, described the move as a political stunt and questioned whether Hasina genuinely intended to return.
According to Reuters, lawyers from London-based Matrix Chambers sent a letter on Monday to Preeti Rahman, acting high commissioner at the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi.
The lawyers requested a new passport and NID for Hasina, citing the reported cancellation of her existing documents by Bangladesh’s interim government and other authorities.
They urged the mission to process the applications expeditiously, referring to her Bangladeshi nationality and obligations under international human rights instruments.
Hasina has previously told Reuters that she intends to return to Bangladesh in December and surrender before a court.
The former prime minister was sentenced to death in absentia by the International Crimes Tribunal in November 2025 over crimes against humanity committed during the crackdown on the 2024 student-led uprising.
She has denied the charges.
Responding to the development at the foreign ministry, State Minister Humaiun Kobir described Hasina’s application as “utterly ridiculous.”
He said Bangladesh would not issue an ordinary passport to facilitate the return of a fugitive convicted of serious crimes.
The state minister stressed that Bangladesh and India already had an extradition treaty and that Hasina’s return should be handled under that agreement.
“If she genuinely wants to return to Bangladesh, she should ask the Indian government to hand her over under the extradition treaty,” he said.
Kobir also criticised the British law firm representing Hasina, questioning the legal and ethical grounds for pursuing the application.
He acknowledged that individuals could engage lawyers and submit representations to authorities, but said doing so did not automatically establish entitlement to a passport.
According to media, diplomatic sources also questioned whether the application had been properly authorised, saying the email did not include a signed authorisation from Hasina.
The Bangladesh mission in Delhi forwarded the communication to the foreign ministry.
Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed adopted a more procedural position, saying the government was still verifying the reported application.
Speaking to reporters at the Secretariat, he said he had learned about the request through media reports but had not independently confirmed its authenticity.
The foreign and law ministries were examining whether the application had been submitted in accordance with the rules and whether Hasina was legally entitled to apply for the documents, he said.
The review would consider the relevant provisions of passport, citizenship and national identity laws.
Salahuddin reiterated that Bangladesh had already approached India through diplomatic channels seeking Hasina’s return under the bilateral extradition treaty.
He said the government would take the necessary steps after examining the legal issues.
International Crimes Tribunal Chief Prosecutor Md Aminul Islam dismissed the application as an attempt to generate political attention.
“Whatever Sheikh Hasina is doing now is a political stunt. She will not come back,” he told reporters at the tribunal.
He said a formal press conference would be held on Tuesday, November 10, to explain the prosecution’s position on Hasina’s reported willingness to surrender.
The prosecutor’s remarks came as the government continued its efforts to secure the former prime minister’s return to face the consequences of the tribunal’s verdict.

item.title: COP31 opens with leaders under pressure to tackle climate crisis
item.description:
The COP31 climate talks kicked off Monday with an early fight over money as the UN’s chief urged world leaders to “get serious” about tackling the crisis after a year of devastating weather extremes.
Antonio Guterres made his plea as thousands of participants descended on a sprawling expo centre in the Turkish Mediterranean city of Antalya for the UN’s annual two-week climate conference.
The summit comes after a year of punishing heatwaves in Europe, major wildfires in Indonesia and catastrophic floods in Nepal, with an exceptionally strong El Nino weather phenomenon fueling more climate chaos.
“We have entered a new age of climate extremes,” Guterres said in a statement.
The UN secretary-general urged leaders to “get serious by cutting emissions faster, accelerating a just transition from fossil fuels and delivering the finance and protection vulnerable countries need.”
The COP31 opening ceremony opened an hour-and-a-half late without explanation.
Negotiators had been locked in discussions late Sunday over demands by developing nations to include items on climate finance in the official agenda.
“This has already been a difficult start for COP31,” said Jasper Inventor, head of Greenpeace’s COP31 delegation.
Under UN climate agreements, developed countries, which are historically responsible for most greenhouse gas emissions, have provided financial support to help developing nations adapt to climate impacts and transition to cleaner energy. But poorer countries say the sums remain insufficient.
Inventor said developed countries took a “hard line” over whether to include a platform, agreed at COP30 in Brazil last year, aimed at discussing how wealthy nations should provide funds to developing nations.
A source familiar with the talks said the “climate finance work program” would be included in the agenda.
African countries had also pushed for the agenda to include the tripling of adaptation finance, which aims to help poorer nations pay for measures such as building sea walls or planting drought-resistant crops.
The source said there would be no separate agenda point on tripling of adaptation finance but that it would be discussed under other items.
A senior European Union official warned last week that there would be “no political will” for extra funding pledges at COP31.
Observers say few major breakthroughs are expected at COP31 as countries grapple with an oil price shock and geopolitical tensions fuelled by the US war with Iran and Russia’s conflict in Ukraine.
The long-term climate outlook is bleak: the United Nations warned in September that global temperatures were on course to exceed 1.5°C above pre-industrial levels, breaching the most ambitious threshold set by the Paris Agreement.
Turkiye is presiding over COP31, with Australia leading negotiations under an unusual arrangement that settled a dispute over who would host the conference but raised concerns over how it would work.
The two sides have celebrated their cooperation so far, with COP31 President Murat Kurum, who is also Turkiye’s environment minister, and Australian Climate Minister Chris Bowen raising their clasped hands above their heads to applause during the opening ceremony.
The partners have branded the summit as the “implementation COP,” focusing on turning commitments into concrete action after years of pledges and ambitious announcements.
“We know that delay carries one of the heaviest costs in climate action,” Kurum said.
Turkiye is inviting countries to join a voluntary “electrification” pledge to raise the share of global energy demand met by electricity from around 20% today to 35% by 2035.
But the initiative could become a source of friction.
The European Union has called for “clean” electrification, a term that could spark debate over the role of oil, gas and coal in the Turkish proposal.
Countries committed to transition away from fossil fuels in a landmark pact at COP28 in Dubai in 2023 but have struggled to agree on how to turn that pledge into action.
COP30 ended with a deal that made no explicit mention of fossil fuels after oil-producing countries opposed the language.
Instead, Brazil produced a voluntary “roadmap” with proposals for phasing out fossil fuels that each country can tailor to their circumstances.
President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, who will be among leaders addressing COP31 later this week, was due to arrive late Monday, fresh from a re-election win that activists hailed as a victory for climate change.
But climate diplomacy is still missing a major player as climate-sceptic US President Donald Trump has not sent officials to COP31.
A US congressional delegation, however, will come to Antalya, with Democrats beaming after last week’s historic US midterm election win.

item.title: ICT chief prosecutor: Hasina's request for passport, NID card a political stunt
item.description:
Describing the application filed by former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina seeking a new passport and national identity card (NID) as a political stunt, Chief Prosecutor of the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT) Md Aminul Islam on Monday said she would never return to Bangladesh.
He came up with the information while talking to reporters, saying the prosecution would present its official position on the matter at a press conference on Tuesday.
Many media outlets carried reports that Hasina had applied for a new Bangladeshi passport and NID card through the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, India, as part of her reported efforts to return home.
In a letter emailed to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi, which was seen by the Associated Press, Hasina’s counsel urged the top diplomat to take necessary action to provide her with a passport and national identity card.
The letter, sent by London-based law firm Matrix Chambers, asked the mission for the application to be processed “expeditiously” on the basis of Hasina’s Bangladeshi nationality and in accordance with “obligations arising under international human rights instruments.”
Hasina fled to India after student-led protests had forced her from power on August 5, 2024 and had since then remained there.
In 2025, a Bangladeshi special tribunal sentenced her to death for crimes against humanity committed during the mass uprising, ruling that she had been responsible for ordering the crackdown, which left hundreds of people dead and thousands of others injured.
Bangladesh has repeatedly sought Hasina’s extradition, but India has declined to hand her over. She first announced in August her intention to return to Bangladesh in December.

item.title: Dollar prices rise again after brief stability
item.description:
After remaining stable between Tk120 and Tk122 for a long time, the price of the US dollar has started rising again.
Within a span of a week, the price of each dollar to settle import liabilities has increased by nearly Tk1.
Currently, the interbank exchange rate stands at Tk124.35 per dollar.
In some cases, the rate for settling import letters of credit (LCs) has exceeded Tk124.90.
In the open market, buyers are having to shell out over Tk128 per dollar.
This market pressure has been generated due to the requirement of additional dollars to settle import liabilities for fuel oil, liquefied natural gas (LNG), and other commodities.
Although export and remittance earnings have increased against this backdrop, the supply of dollars is failing to keep pace with demand.
Data on foreign exchange transactions from Bangladesh Bank also reveals a widening gap between import and export earnings.
During the first three months (July–September) of the current FY27, merchandise import expenses reached $1.933 billion.
Compared to the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year, these expenses rose by 15.10%.
Conversely, export earnings grew by 7%. During this period, $1.186 billion came from exports, resulting in a trade deficit of $7.47 billion for the three months.
In the same period of the previous fiscal year, this deficit was $5.71 billion.
This means the trade deficit has increased by $1.76 billion within a year.
Petroleum products played the largest role behind this upward trend in import expenses.
In the first quarter, expenses for importing petroleum products exceeded $4.22 billion.
In the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year, expenses in this sector were less than $2.06 billion.
In other words, fuel import expenses have surged by more than 105% in a year.
Bankers stated that this expenditure has grown due to rising global oil prices and purchasing LNG at higher prices from the spot market. Additional dollars are also required to pay off LNG import liabilities.
Along with fuel, the import of essential commodities is also increasing pressure on the dollar market. In the first three months, expenses for consumer goods imports rose by 26.50%, costing the sector $1.40 billion.
Ahead of Ramadan, traders are preparing to open new LCs for items such as edible oil, sugar, lentils, and chickpeas.
Bankers apprehend that this will further drive up the demand for dollars.
On the other hand, capital machinery imports declined by 13.60%. This indicates that while spending on consumer goods and fuel is growing, imports of capital machinery related to production and investment are dropping.
Remedies
To increase the supply of dollars in the market, Bangladesh Bank is selling dollars from its reserves.
Last Wednesday, the central bank sold $120 million to commercial banks through an auction, with exchange rates ranging from Tk124.30 to Tk124.35 per dollar.
However, market pressure cannot be fully managed solely through the supply of dollars from reserves.
According to the latest figures, the country's total foreign exchange reserves have dropped to $34.85 billion.
Meanwhile, Bangladesh Bank has warned commercial banks regarding the rising trend in dollar prices.
Recently, during a meeting with the managing directors of banks, Governor Md Mostaqur Rahman stated that dollar prices should not rise to such an extent given that banks' net open position (NOP) remains positive.
He emphasized the need to remain vigilant so that no party can create instability in the market under the pretext of a crisis.
Arief Hossain Khan, executive director and spokesperson of Bangladesh Bank, told reporters that the central bank is examining whether coordinating institutions and bankers have any role beyond logical reasons behind the hike in dollar prices. Action will be taken if anyone's involvement is found.
Regarding the price hike of dollars in the open market, MS Zaman, president of the Money Changers Association of Bangladesh, said that dollar prices have increased everywhere, including banks.
A sudden surge in demand has caused some supply issues, but he hoped that the situation will normalize soon.

item.title: Consumers Forum: Essential goods prices rise by 4.39% in October
item.description:
Prices of essential commodities across the country increased by an average of 4.39% in October, driven largely by a sharp hike in fish and spice prices, according to findings by the Consumers Forum (CF).
Data compiled by the organization across various markets in Dhaka—including Karwan Bazar, Rampura, Meradia, Aftabnagar's Bhuiyan Bazar, and several super shops—showed that prices of 15 key categories of goods rose during the month.
Fish prices recorded the highest surge, jumping by an average of 11.72%.
Prices of spices, including cloves, cardamom, cinnamon, and cumin, rose by 10.30%, while onions, garlic, and ginger saw a 7.79% increase.
Other notable price hikes included fuel oil (6.02%), sugar (4.93%), edible oil and dalda (4.80%), flour and maida (3.25%), rice (2.62%), eggs (1.42%), meat (0.38%), and tea (0.14%).
Conversely, prices of seven essential items, including salt, dairy products, toothpaste, biscuits, 11 major brands of medicines, and stationery items, remained stable.
Meanwhile, prices dropped for two categories: vegetables fell by 3.12% and gold and silver by 4.77%.
Field reports from different parts of the vegetable supply hub, including Jessore, Bogra, and Rangpur, indicated that winter vegetables have begun arriving in local wholesale markets, though producers are struggling to recover their production costs.
While cauliflower and cabbage sold for Tk6–12, radishes for Tk6–8, gourds for Tk8–10, and plantains for Tk5–8 per 4-piece (hali) locally in regions like Bogra and Rangpur, they were retailed at much higher prices in Dhaka, with cauliflowers and cabbages fetching around Tk50, papayas and radishes Tk30, gourds Tk60, and plantains Tk40–50 per hali.
According to the Consumers Forum, essential commodity prices had already risen by 3.13% in September, bringing the cumulative two-month increase to 7.52%.
In a press release issued Sunday by CF General Secretary Emdad Hossain Malek, the organization emphasized that merely raising wages is insufficient.
It called on authorities to keep essential living expenses—including urban house and shop rents, education, and healthcare—within the purchasing power of middle and lower-middle-income groups.
The forum urged strict administrative and legal actions to curb excessive profit-seeking by unscrupulous traders and safeguard public welfare.

item.title: President: Govt rebuilding collapsed education system, democratic institutions
item.description:
President Mirza Fakhrul Islam Alamgir on Monday said the government has been working to rebuild education system and democratic institutions, collapsed during the ousted fascist government.
"Over the last one and half decades, the education system and democratic institutions were dismantled. The current government is working to reorganize and rebuild them afresh," he said.
The president said this when a delegation of American International University-Bangladesh (AIUB), led by its founding member and Board of Trustees Chairman Dr Hasanul A Hasan, paid a courtesy call on him at Bangabhaban on Monday morning, President's Press Secretary Md. Sarwar Alam told BSS.
During the meeting, AIUB Vice-Chancellor Prof Dr Saiful Islam briefed the president on the university's overall educational, research and academic activities, as well as its position in international rankings.
The president assured the delegation of his cooperation and support when the delegation drew President's attention about various problems and needs of the university.
The AIUB authorities also invited the president to attend the university's proposed convocation ceremony and the chancellor and president assured them of his presence at the convocation.
The president's military secretary, secretary and press secretary, along with members of the university's Board of Trustees, were present at the meeting.

item.title: Sheikh Hasina faces 673 cases, including 457 murder cases
item.description:
A total of 673 lawsuits, including 457 on murder charges, have been filed against former Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina, who was ousted from power in the July mass uprising, according to police headquarters data.

She has been sentenced to death in one case involving crimes against humanity committed during the July uprising. Six more cases against her are pending trial at the International Crimes Tribunal (ICT).

Reuters has reported that a letter has been sent to the Bangladesh High Commission in New Delhi seeking a new passport and national identity (NID) card for Sheikh Hasina, who has been staying in India since the mass uprising in August 2024.

Diplomatic sources informed Prothom Alo that the Bangladesh High Commission received an email regarding the passport and NID. However, the sources also said the email was not accompanied by an authorisation letter from Sheikh Hasina. Against this backdrop, the cases against her and her death sentence have come into renewed focus.

Following the fall of the government of Awami League (whose activities are currently banned in the country) in the mass uprising on 5 August 2024, the then interim government reconstituted the ICT. An arrest warrant was issued against Sheikh Hasina on 17 October 2024, the first day of proceedings at the reconstituted tribunal.

The verdict in that case was delivered on 17 November 2025. The International Crimes Tribunal-1 sentenced Sheikh Hasina and former home minister Asaduzzaman Khan to death for crimes against humanity, committed during the July mass uprising. Former Inspector General of Police (IGP), Chowdhury Abdullah Al-Mamun, who turned approver, was sentenced to five years in prison.

Bangladesh Police has also applied for an Interpol Red Notice against Sheikh Hasina. In April 2025, the National Central Bureau (NCB) of Bangladesh Police submitted applications for Red Notices against 12 people, including Sheikh Hasina. However, no Red Notice has been issued.

On 27 August, incumbent Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed informed the Jatiya Sangsad (national parliament) that a formal extradition request had been sent to India seeking Sheikh Hasina’s return. An application had also been submitted to Interpol for a Red Notice.

Hasina did not appeal

The full verdict in the case in which Sheikh Hasina was sentenced to death was published on 13 January. The International Crimes Tribunal Act allows 30 days to file an appeal. However, Sheikh Hasina did not appeal within the stipulated period. Tribunal sources said she was no longer eligible to appeal as the deadline had expired.

Alongside the death sentences, the tribunal ordered the confiscation of the properties owned by Sheikh Hasina and Asaduzzaman Khan in Bangladesh in favour of the state. It also ordered compensation for the families of those killed and those injured during the July mass uprising.

On 3 November, the Office of the Chief Prosecutor of the tribunal sent a letter to the home ministry to implement the confiscation order. It requested the preparation of a comprehensive list of the movable and immovable assets of the two convicts and their transfer to state control.

6 more crimes against humanity cases

Six more cases involving crimes against humanity against Sheikh Hasina are pending before the tribunal. Of these, two are at the witness examination stage and four are at the charge-framing stage. Arrest warrants have been issued against her in all six cases.

Sheikh Hasina and 16 others have been accused in a case over enforced disappearances at the Task Force for Interrogation (TFI) cell of the Rapid Action Battalion (RAB). Among the accused are 12 serving and former military officers.

In another case involving enforced disappearances at the Joint Interrogation Cell (JIC) of the Directorate General of Forces Intelligence (DGFI), 13 people have been accused. Apart from Sheikh Hasina, the other 12 accused are serving and former military officers. Both cases are at the witness examination stage.

Sheikh Hasina and 40 others have been accused in a crimes against humanity case over killings surrounding a Hefazat-e-Islam rally at Shapla Chattar in Motijheel, Dhaka, on 5 May 2013.

In another case over the killing of former municipal councillor Ekramul Haque, reportedly in a gunfight in Teknaf of Cox’s Bazar on 26 May 2018, Sheikh Hasina and 10 others have been accused. Both cases are currently at the charge-framing stage.

Two other cases are at the hearing stage for charge framing before Tribunal-2.

One concerns the alleged killing of nine youths in Kalyanpur of Dhaka in 2016, in what prosecutors describe as a staged anti-militancy operation. Sheikh Hasina and seven others have been accused in the case.

In another case over the killing of seven people in a purported anti-militancy operation at Patartek in Gazipur, Sheikh Hasina and nine others have been accused.

International Crimes Tribunal prosecutor Mizanul Islam told Prothom Alo that an arrest warrant remained in force against Sheikh Hasina. It would be carried out if she returned to the country, he said.

She would also have to face trial in the cases pending against her before the tribunal, Mizanul Islam added.

item.title: Tarique-Erdogan meeting in Antalya today as Dhaka-Ankara ties grow closer
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman will meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan in Antalya, Türkiye, today, Tuesday.

The two leaders are scheduled to meet at 6:30pm local time at the Maxx Royal Hotel in Antalya. Diplomatic sources in Dhaka confirmed the information to Prothom Alo.

According to diplomatic sources in Dhaka, since the BNP government took office, relations between Dhaka and Ankara have grown closer through reciprocal visits by the two countries' foreign ministers, a visit to Türkiye by the Bangladesh Army chief and high-level contacts. Today's meeting is a continuation of that process.

Prime Minister Tarique Rahman left Dhaka for Antalya this morning to attend the United Nations climate change conference (COP31). During the official visit from 10 to 12 November, the prime minister will lead the Bangladesh delegation. He will deliver Bangladesh's statement at the plenary session of the conference on 12 November.

On the sidelines of the conference, Prime Minister Tarique Rahman may hold bilateral meetings with the leaders of several countries, including the Turkish president.

This will be Tarique Rahman's second meeting with President Erdogan since he took office as prime minister.

The two leaders first met at the Turkish House in New York on 22 September, on the sidelines of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly. At the meeting, Erdogan called for placing bilateral relations on a more institutional footing. He emphasised expanding cooperation in the defence industry and increasing bilateral trade.

In early June, Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan visited Dhaka. On the final day of his visit, he paid a courtesy call on Prime Minister Tarique Rahman. During the meeting, Fidan said his visit was the first step towards elevating relations between the two countries to a strategic level.

Following the meeting, the two countries announced the formation of a joint committee at the ministerial level on defence and foreign affairs. The two sides also agreed to hold annual meetings between their foreign ministers and regular meetings involving the foreign and defence ministers.

During his visit to Dhaka, Fidan held a joint press conference with Bangladesh Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman. Khalilur Rahman thanked Türkiye for supporting Bangladesh's bid for the presidency of the 81st session of the United Nations General Assembly.

Contacts between the two countries in the defence sector have increased over the past few years.

In July, Bangladesh Army Chief General Waker-Uz-Zaman visited Türkiye. During the five-day official visit, meetings focused on the existing friendly relations between the two countries, bilateral defence cooperation, military training, defence technology, cooperation in the defence industry, capacity building and various issues of mutual interest.

Both sides expressed interest in further expanding professional ties, exchanging experiences and strengthening defence cooperation between their armed forces in the future. As part of the visit, the army chief also inspected the operations of several leading defence industry and military technology institutions in Türkiye.

The Rohingya issue also features in Bangladesh–Türkiye discussions. At the meeting in New York, Erdogan praised Bangladesh for sheltering more than one million Rohingya. He expressed his country's commitment to continuing humanitarian assistance in areas including shelter, education and infrastructure for the Rohingya.

High-level contacts between the two countries have increased since the BNP government took office in February. Türkiye was represented at the swearing-in ceremony on 17 February by Deputy Foreign Minister Beris Ekinci.

After taking office, Foreign Minister Khalilur Rahman made his first bilateral visit to Turkey on 14 March. During his meeting with Hakan Fidan in Ankara, a memorandum of understanding was signed between the diplomatic training institutes of the two countries. Khalilur Rahman also attended the Antalya Diplomacy Forum from 17 to 19 April. Hakan Fidan made his first visit to Dhaka in June.

item.title: Economy and reforms: LDC graduation window extended, challenges remain
item.description:
USA-TRUMP-TARIFFS-BANGLADESH-FACTORY

On 29 October 2026, during the 81st Session of the United Nations General Assembly UNGA), a decision was adopted to grant Bangladesh an additional three years to prepare for its graduation from the Least Developed Country (LDC) category. Consequently, Bangladesh will now potentially graduate from the LDC group on 24 November 2029 instead of 24 November 2026.

This decision accords Bangladesh vital extra time to prepare. It also creates an opportunity to retain international support measures and trade preferences accorded to LDCs for a longer period. However, additional time alone will not eliminate the structural vulnerabilities of the economy. For that, concrete actions and tough decisions are imperative. Bangladesh must leverage this opportunity to execute significant and effective economic reforms.

The UN Committee for Development Policy (CDP) reviews the progress of LDCs every three years based on three criteria: Per Capita Gross National Income (GNI), the Human Assets Index (HAI), and the Economic and Environmental Vulnerability Index (EVI). A country is considered for graduation if it meets the requisite thresholds in two consecutive triennial reviews. Bangladesh met these criteria for the first time in 2018 and again in 2021, prompting the CDP to recommend its graduation from the LDC category.

In view of the severe damage inflicted on the economy and development trajectory by the Covid-19 pandemic, the UN exceptionally granted Bangladesh, Laos, and Nepal a five-year preparatory period. As per the UN General Assembly resolution of 24 November 2021, Bangladesh’s graduation date was initially fixed for 24 November 2026. Under the latest decision, Bangladesh and Nepal have been granted a further three-year extension.

This additional timeframe offers Bangladesh a strategic window to address readiness gaps and implement plans for mitigating post-graduation challenges. During the preparatory phase, certain international support measures and trade benefits available to LDCs may continue under existing rules. However, uniform privileges will not apply across all markets, nor will the duration of these benefits be identical. Therefore, Bangladesh must immediately initiate bilateral engagements with its major trading partners. In particular, it must seek clarity regarding post-graduation tariff rates, rules of origin, and market access conditions.

The burden of enhancing competitiveness cannot rest on exporters alone. If the costs of power, energy, transport, logistics, customs clearance, and financing remain prohibitive, businesses cannot reduce unit production costs unassisted. The government must elevate the quality of these public services, while facilitating access to easy financing, technical advice, skill development programmes, and streamlined product certification systems.

To remain competitive in international markets, relying solely on duty-free access will not suffice. Prolonged port clearance delays, high transport costs, uninterrupted energy shortages, complex customs procedures, low productivity, and a narrow export basket must be addressed urgently. Operational efficiency at ports and in transport networks must be enhanced. Production lead times and costs must be curtailed. International labour rights and environmental standards must be upheld. Concurrently, businesses should be incentivised to produce higher value-added goods. Exporters also require targeted support to comply with rules of origin and technical requirements in global markets.

In this context, trade agreements can play a pivotal role. Bangladesh has already entered into several trade negotiations, notably the Economic Partnership Agreement (EPA) with Japan and the Comprehensive Economic Partnership Agreement (CEPA) with South Korea, both of which represent positive steps forward. However, before signing further agreements, the market dynamics of prospective partner countries, high-potential sectors, and specific contractual terms must be rigorously evaluated.

These agreements should look beyond mere import-export tariffs to encompass trade in services, investment, customs clearance, product standards, rules of origin, digital trade, and technological cooperation. Yet, signing agreements does not automatically equate to success. The true benchmark of success will lie in the extent to which export volumes and investment inflows increase, new technologies are transferred, and domestic enterprises benefit.

Bangladesh’s export basket remains overwhelmingly dependent on ready-made garments (RMG). Diversifying away from this concentration to boost non-RMG exports is critical. Potential exists to expand exports in pharmaceuticals, leather goods, processed agricultural products, light engineering goods, and IT-enabled services. Achieving this requires manufacturing goods to international standards, building a skilled workforce, ensuring uninterrupted power and energy supplies, modernising transport logistics, and reducing the cost of doing business. Furthermore, small and medium enterprises (SMEs) require financial and technological assistance to enable their entry into new export markets.

The burden of enhancing competitiveness cannot rest on exporters alone. If the costs of power, energy, transport, logistics, customs clearance, and financing remain prohibitive, businesses cannot reduce unit production costs unassisted. The government must elevate the quality of these public services, while facilitating access to easy financing, technical advice, skill development programmes, and streamlined product certification systems. Such measures will enable commercial enterprises to adopt modern machinery, conserve energy, minimise waste, and boost productivity, thereby creating new product lines to penetrate wider markets.

Reforming the import tariff regime is equally crucial. A major share of the government’s revenue is derived from import-stage taxes. However, high tariffs and supplementary duties inflate the import costs of raw materials and machinery for export-oriented industries, This in turn drives up production costs and erodes competitiveness in international markets.

That is why, tariff structures must be gradually simplified and rationalised through a clear, medium-term roadmap. Unnecessary tariff slabs should be consolidated, aligning duty structures with production and export needs. However, an abrupt reduction in tariffs could undermine government revenue. To offset this, revenue collection from direct income tax and Value Added Tax (VAT) must be enhanced by broadening the tax base and improving the efficiency of tax administration. Reducing reliance on import taxes will safeguard public spending in critical sectors such as education, health, and emergency infrastructure.

The extension of Bangladesh’s LDC graduation timeline comes at a juncture when the domestic economy has been grappling with multi-year headwinds. Under current circumstances, restoring macroeconomic stability must remain the paramount priority. Controlling inflation, bolstering revenue generation, mitigating external sector pressures, and enforcing good governance in the banking sector are indispensable for stimulating investment and production. Resolving these challenges demands deep-seated structural reforms.

The government’s Smooth Transition Strategy (STS) for LDC graduation must also be rigorously implemented. Its primary objective should be to preserve Bangladesh's export competitiveness, employment levels, and development momentum as LDC-specific preferences are phased out. The extra three years must not be viewed merely as a deferral of the deadline; this period must be utilised effectively to rectify economic vulnerabilities, enhance productivity, and prepare Bangladesh for international competition.

* Fahmida Khatun is an economist and Distinguished Fellow at the Centre for Policy Dialogue (CPD)

item.title: UNFCCC COP31: Zero waste, food security and resilient cities for Bangladesh
item.description:
CLIMATE-COP31/

The world looks to the 31st Conference of the Parties to the United Nations Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC COP31), being held on 9–20 November  2026, in Antalya, Türkiye. Bangladesh faces a critical question: how can global climate commitments translate into tangible benefits for its people, food systems and cities?

For a country on the frontlines of climate change, the answers lie not only in reducing emissions but also in embracing zero-waste approaches, safeguarding food security and building resilient cities. These priorities are deeply interconnected, offering Bangladesh a practical pathway to cut emissions, reduce environmental pollution, protect livelihoods and strengthen its resilience to a changing climate. 

Co-led by Türkiye and Australia, COP31 is placing greater emphasis on implementation, investment and practical action. Its Action Agenda identifies ten priorities: Climate Implementation Bridge, Clean Energy Transition, Green Industrialization, Climate-Resilient Cities, Oceans and Seas, Food Security, Zero Waste, Dynamic and Resilient Health Systems, Rio Synergies, and Youth and Education.

For Bangladesh, these priorities are directly connected to national development. The country must reduce greenhouse gas emissions while protecting people from floods, cyclones, rising temperatures, salinity intrusion and other climate hazards. It must also safeguard food security, create jobs and improve public health.

Three areas deserve particular attention: Zero Waste, Food Security and Climate-Resilient Cities. Together, they offer practical opportunities to reduce methane and carbon emissions while strengthening the resilience of communities and ecosystems.

From climate pledges to implementation

Bangladesh's Third Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC 3.0), submitted in September 2025, sets a target of reducing greenhouse gas emissions by 20.31 per cent below the business-as-usual scenario by 2035. This includes a 6.39 per cent reduction through domestic resources and a further 13.92 per cent reduction conditional on international support.

Achieving these targets will require coordinated action across energy, industry, agriculture, transport and waste management. Expanding renewable energy, improving industrial energy efficiency, promoting cleaner production and reducing fossil fuel consumption can help lower emissions while supporting economic growth.

However, the financial challenge is substantial. Bangladesh estimates that implementing its NDC mitigation measures during 2026–2035 will require approximately US$116.18 billion. Of this amount, US$25.95 billion is associated with unconditional actions to be financed through domestic resources, while US$90.23 billion depends on international climate finance.

These figures demonstrate the gap between climate ambition and available resources. Bangladesh cannot reasonably be expected to finance the entire transition from its own limited public resources while also addressing poverty, infrastructure deficits and the growing costs of climate adaptation.

At COP31, Bangladesh should call for predictable, accessible and additional climate finance, together with technology transfer and capacity building. It must also strengthen its ability to develop investment-ready projects, supported by clear budgets, implementation plans, measurable outcomes and transparent monitoring.

Zero Waste: An opportunity to cut methane

Waste management is often treated as a municipal cleanliness issue. In reality, it is also a climate priority.

When food scraps and other biodegradable materials decompose without sufficient oxygen in unmanaged dumpsites and landfills, they release methane. Methane is a powerful greenhouse gas that contributes significantly to near-term global warming. Reducing these emissions can deliver important climate benefits while improving environmental health.

Bangladesh's rapidly growing cities generate large quantities of household waste, market refuse, food scraps and discarded packaging. Inadequate collection and disposal systems contribute to pollution, blocked drainage, contaminated waterways and public health risks. Organic waste deposited in unmanaged disposal sites adds to the country's methane burden.

The answer is not simply to build more landfills. Nor should waste incineration become the default solution. Bangladesh needs a waste management system that prioritises prevention, reuse, repair, recycling and the recovery of organic materials, with safe disposal reserved for residual waste.

Municipalities should introduce waste segregation at source and expand composting and appropriately designed anaerobic digestion. Composting can return nutrients to agricultural soils, while anaerobic digestion can capture biogas from organic waste for productive use.

These measures must be supported by reliable collection services, recycling infrastructure and stronger producer responsibility. Manufacturers should take greater responsibility for the packaging and products they introduce into the market. Informal waste workers, who already play a significant role in material recovery, must also be included in formal waste management systems and protected through fair working conditions.

For Bangladesh, Zero Waste is not simply about reducing rubbish. It can cut methane emissions, create green jobs, reduce pressure on landfills, conserve resources and protect rivers and wetlands from pollution.

The government should integrate measurable waste-related methane reduction targets into national and municipal climate plans, supported by emissions baselines, clear institutional responsibilities and adequate financing.

Food security is climate security

Agriculture remains central to Bangladesh's economy, rural livelihoods and food security. Yet rising temperatures, erratic rainfall, floods, droughts and salinity intrusion threaten agricultural productivity and the stability of food supplies.

Climate shocks can damage crops, disrupt transport and storage, increase food prices and deepen the vulnerability of low-income households. These risks make climate-resilient agriculture an urgent national priority.

Food waste adds another dimension to the problem. When food is lost during harvesting, transportation, storage and distribution, the resources used to produce it are also wasted. If discarded food decomposes in unmanaged dumpsites, it generates additional methane.

Bangladesh should therefore connect food security, agricultural resilience and waste prevention through a coordinated approach.

Priority actions include developing flood-, drought- and salinity-tolerant crop varieties, improving irrigation efficiency, strengthening agricultural extension services, expanding climate information for farmers and investing in better storage and transportation infrastructure.

Methane reduction should also become an integral part of agricultural policy. Where local conditions permit, alternate wetting and drying in rice cultivation can reduce methane emissions. Improved livestock feeding, better manure management and biogas systems can offer further benefits.

At the same time, markets, restaurants, institutions and households should take practical steps to prevent avoidable food waste. Better storage, more efficient distribution, food donation arrangements and the separate collection of unavoidable organic waste can reduce losses throughout the food system.

These measures must not place additional financial burdens on small farmers. Access to affordable credit, technical assistance, appropriate technologies and practical incentives will be essential.

Bangladesh must demonstrate that reducing emissions and protecting food production are complementary goals. A climate policy that undermines farmers' livelihoods or threatens food affordability cannot be sustainable.

Building climate-resilient, low-carbon cities

Bangladesh's urban centres face a growing combination of extreme heat, air pollution, traffic congestion, flooding, inadequate drainage and the loss of wetlands and natural water channels. Rapid, poorly planned urbanisation is intensifying these problems while increasing energy demand and emissions.

The COP31 priority on Climate-Resilient Cities provides an opportunity to integrate climate adaptation and mitigation into urban planning.

Bangladesh should prioritise energy-efficient buildings, rooftop solar, improved public transport, safe walking and cycling infrastructure, better drainage, restored canals and wetlands, and expanded urban green spaces. These investments can reduce emissions while protecting people from heat and flooding.

Waste and sanitation must also be central to urban climate policy. Poorly managed organic waste and wastewater can contribute to greenhouse gas emissions, while inadequate treatment threatens public health and water quality.

Municipal authorities should improve sewage and wastewater treatment, strengthen faecal sludge management and establish reliable systems for collecting and treating organic waste. Methane baselines should be developed for major waste and sanitation hotspots so that reductions can be measured over time.

Urban development must also protect natural systems. Wetlands, canals, rivers and urban trees provide flood storage, moderate temperatures, support biodiversity and improve the quality of life. Destroying these systems in the name of development often creates greater long-term economic and environmental costs.

The goal should be to make cities both low-carbon and climate-resilient. Efficient buildings reduce energy consumption; better public transport lowers fuel use; restored wetlands reduce flood risks; and improved sanitation protects communities from pollution and disease.

For Bangladesh, these are not separate environmental interventions. They are essential investments in public health, economic productivity and urban security.

Making climate finance work

The Climate Implementation Bridge is particularly relevant to Bangladesh because it emphasises the need to connect national climate commitments with financing and practical implementation.

Bangladesh should use COP31 to develop a coordinated portfolio of projects in renewable energy, industrial efficiency, methane reduction, climate-smart agriculture, waste recovery and resilient urban infrastructure.

This requires stronger coordination among the ministries responsible for environment, energy, agriculture, finance and local government. Climate priorities must be reflected in national budgets, sectoral investment plans and local development programmes.

Reliable emissions inventories, methane baselines and transparent monitoring systems are equally important. They will help the country identify where investment can deliver the greatest benefits and demonstrate whether projects are achieving their intended results.

Public finance should also be used strategically to encourage private investment in clean energy, recycling, composting and other low-carbon services. However, private investment cannot replace grants and highly concessional finance for essential public goods such as flood protection, wetland restoration and sanitation in vulnerable communities.

Zero Waste, Food Security and Climate-Resilient Cities are closely connected. Better waste management can reduce methane and protect waterways

International climate finance must be accessible, timely and consistent with the principle of equity. Bangladesh should assess financing not only by the amounts pledged but also by how much is disbursed, the terms offered and the benefits delivered.

Bangladesh must turn ambition into action

Bangladesh should approach COP31 with a dual strategy: press for the international support needed to meet its climate commitments while demonstrating its readiness to implement practical and measurable solutions.

Zero Waste, Food Security and Climate-Resilient Cities are closely connected. Better waste management can reduce methane and protect waterways. Climate-resilient agriculture can safeguard food supplies while reducing avoidable emissions. Better-planned cities can lower energy consumption while protecting communities from heat, floods and pollution.

Achieving these objectives will require capable institutions, adequate financing, effective enforcement and meaningful participation by local governments, research institutions, civil society, businesses and communities. Young people should be recognised as partners in climate action, scientific innovation and environmental decision-making.

Bangladesh has valuable experience in disaster preparedness, community adaptation and environmental advocacy. It can use that experience to contribute to international climate cooperation while demonstrating how a developing country can pursue economic growth alongside lower emissions and greater resilience.

Ultimately, COP31 should be judged not by the number of commitments announced but by the results countries achieve. For Bangladesh, success must mean less methane, cleaner cities, more resilient food systems, healthier ecosystems and climate finance that reaches the communities that need it most.

The challenge is to bridge the gap between climate ambition and implementation. Bangladesh must turn its commitments into investments, its investments into measurable emission reductions, and its climate policies into lasting improvements in people's lives.

* Dr. Shahriar Hossain is an environmental scientist, journalist, and social justice advocate. He serves as Secretary General of the Environment and Social Development Organization (ESDO) and contributes to international environmental policy, conventions, and advocacy.

item.description:
A total of 22 vehicles were set on fire across the country in the past 24 hours.

During this period, miscreants exploded crude bombs at at least 28 locations in Dhaka and six other districts.

Sources at the Police Headquarters and Dhaka Metropolitan Police (DMP) said vehicles were set on fire in 11 districts, both in and outside Dhaka.

The incidents took place between Monday morning and Tuesday morning.

Meanwhile, a police vehicle was set on fire, roads were blocked and shops were vandalised in Gopalganj today, Tuesday.

Over the past three days, a series of acts of sabotage have been reported across the country.

Against this backdrop, Inspector General of Police (IGP) Ali Hossain Fakir held a meeting with the superintendents of police (SPs) of all 64 districts.

He instructed them to arrest those involved in sabotage, intensify patrols and strengthen intelligence surveillance.

All metropolitan police commissioners and deputy inspectors general (DIGs) of police ranges were also present at the meeting.

Additional police personnel have been ordered to be deployed in four districts—Gopalganj, Shariatpur, Madaripur and Faridpur.

A police source said that leaders and activists of the party of ousted prime minister Sheikh Hasina had been carrying out acts of sabotage across the country centring on her announcement that she would return to Bangladesh.

Leaders who have fled abroad are instigating these activities and sending money to fund sabotage, the source added. Names of those behind the incidents have reportedly emerged during the interrogation of people recently arrested in connection with sabotage.

Officials concerned said that eight to nine crude bombs exploded at different locations of Dhaka University within a short period on Sunday evening. Three people were arrested on the spot in connection with the incidents.

The arrested individuals are from Gopalganj, Rajshahi and Naogaon. None of them is directly involved in the politics of the Awami League whose activities are currently banned. They carried out the activities in exchange for money.

However, most of those arrested in Dhaka and elsewhere in the country over the past 24 hours are directly involved in the politics of the Awami League and its affiliated organisations.

According to Police Headquarters data, 29 people were arrested between Saturday and Monday in connection with acts of sabotage in different parts of the country.

Assistant Inspector General (AIG) Kamarum Munira, spokesperson for Police Headquarters, told Prothom Alo that planned activities by criminals were behind recent acts of sabotage, including cocktail bomb explosions and arson attacks, in different parts of the country.

She further said that measures were being taken to prevent sabotage through increased intelligence surveillance, intensified patrols and checkpoints in vulnerable areas, public cooperation, CCTV and cyber monitoring, and coordination among intelligence agencies.

Necessary steps were also being taken to identify and bring to justice those involved in each incident.

She said greater emphasis was being placed not only on taking action after incidents but also on collecting information, assessing risks and taking preventive measures beforehand, she added.

Vehicles set on fire in 11 districts

According to Police Headquarters data, miscreants set fire to four vehicles in Dhaka metropolitan area in the past 24 hours. Three vehicles were also set on fire in Chattogram metropolitan area. In addition, 15 vehicles were set on fire in Narayanganj, Naogaon, Gazipur, Patuakhali, Mymensingh, Gaibandha, Satkhira, Bogura, Manikganj, South Keraniganj in Dhaka district and Faridpur. Two vehicles each were set on fire in Narayanganj, Gazipur and Mymensingh.

DMP sources said miscreants set fire to two parked buses in the capital's Farmgate and Pallabi areas on Monday night. In addition, two mini-trucks were set on fire on Sadarghat Road in Old Dhaka late Monday night.

Crude bombs explode at 19 locations in Dhaka

According to DMP sources, reports of cocktail bomb explosions at 19 locations in Dhaka were received between Monday afternoon and Tuesday morning. Police have arrested at least 33 people in connection with these incidents.

Outside Dhaka, miscreants detonated cocktail bombs in Manikganj, Gopalganj, Chattogram, Shariatpur, Cox's Bazar and Rangpur.

DMP spokesperson Deputy Commissioner Akhtar Hossain told Prothom Alo that many people involved in sabotage had already been arrested. Security had been strengthened across the city and patrols intensified, he added.

Increased surveillance in four districts

Clashes and counter-chases took place between police and leaders and activists of the banned Chhatra League in Tungipara, Gopalganj. During the incidents, a police vehicle was set on fire and several shops were vandalised. Several people, including police personnel, were injured in the clashes.

Meanwhile, leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and its affiliated organisations blocked roads by setting fires at various locations in Kashiani upazila. Roads were also blocked on the western side of Launch Ghat Bridge, in the Sonakur area and at the LGED intersection in Gopalganj town. These incidents took place at various locations in Tungipara, Kashiani and Sadar upazilas from Tuesday morning.

Earlier, late Monday night, leaders and activists of the banned Awami League and Chhatra League blocked a road in front of the toll plaza at the Zajira end of the Padma Bridge, carrying logs and oars. Several crude bombs exploded and trucks were vandalised during the incident.

Following these incidents, additional police personnel have been deployed in Gopalganj, Shariatpur, Madaripur and Faridpur.

Police Headquarters has also instructed the superintendents of police in these four districts to intensify patrols and intelligence surveillance.

Sources concerned said they had been asked to remain alert to prevent people from gathering in large numbers and carrying out major acts of sabotage.

Instructions against mass arrests

IGP Ali Hossain Fakir held an online meeting with senior police officials from across the country from Police Headquarters today. At the meeting, he instructed them to arrest those involved in recent acts of sabotage.

However, the IGP told the superintendents of police not to resort to mass arrests as was done during the previous Awami League government.

After the meeting, Prothom Alo spoke to the superintendents of police of three districts. The senior district police officials said the IGP had instructed them to ensure “quality arrests”, meaning the arrest of actual perpetrators. item.title: PM arrives in Antalya for COP31 summit
item.description:
Prime Minister Tarique Rahman arrived in Türkiye’s Antalya on Tuesday afternoon to attend the World Leaders’ Summit of the 31st Conference of the Parties (COP31) and hold bilateral meetings with leaders of different countries.
A Turkish Airlines flight carrying the prime minister, his wife Dr Zubaida Rahman and members of his entourage landed at Antalya Airport at 4:05pm local time, said his Deputy Press Secretary Hasan Shiplu.
The flight made a brief stopover in Istanbul after departing Hazrat Shahjalal International Airport in Dhaka at 7:30am Bangladesh time. It was scheduled to leave Istanbul at 2:45pm local time.
The prime minister is scheduled to meet Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdoğan at 6:30pm local time at Maxx Royal Hotel, according to his tour schedule and foreign ministry sources.
COP31 began in Antalya on Monday and will continue until November 20. The two-day World Leaders’ Summit is scheduled for November 11-12.
Tarique is scheduled to address a plenary session on November 12 and hold several bilateral meetings on the sidelines of the summit, Foreign Secretary Salahuddin Noman Chowdhury said at a briefing in Dhaka on Monday.
The prime minister is expected to outline Bangladesh’s position and priorities on climate justice, the historical responsibility of developed countries, climate finance, adaptation, loss and damage, and climate-resilient sustainable development.
The foreign secretary said Bangladesh’s priorities include securing adaptation finance, addressing loss and damage, and ensuring effective implementation of developed countries’ climate finance commitments.
Although Bangladesh accounts for only 0.05% of global greenhouse gas emissions, it remains among the countries most vulnerable to climate change, he said, stressing that securing climate justice is a key priority.
Bangladesh will also highlight its achievements in climate resilience and share its experience in addressing climate impacts across South Asia and the wider Asian region.
The country has taken an initiative to establish a jute pavilion in the conference’s Green Zone to showcase the versatility of jute, its environment-friendly properties and its potential as an alternative to plastic.
A joint declaration between Bangladesh and Türkiye on the use and promotion of jute and jute products is also expected to be signed during the conference, the foreign secretary said.
The foreign ministry will organise two side events in the Blue Zone on November 12 and 13. One will focus on gender-based vulnerability in Bangladesh caused by climate change, while the other will address challenges in promoting environment-friendly, biodegradable and zero-waste jute products.
The prime minister is scheduled to leave Antalya for Dhaka at 4:15pm local time on November 12. The flight is expected to arrive in Dhaka at 5:50am on November 13.

item.title: IPCC chief urges COP31 to break deadlock over climate reports
item.description:
Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change (IPCC) Chair Jim Skea has urged governments attending COP31 to resolve a deadlock over the schedule and budget for the panel’s next major scientific assessments, warning that delays are disrupting researchers’ work and threatening the timely delivery of critical climate findings.
Speaking at the ceremonial opening of COP31 on Monday, Skea said governments had yet to agree on the timetable and funding for three major reports under the IPCC’s Seventh Assessment Report (AR7).
The assessments will cover the physical science of climate change, its impacts and adaptation, and options for reducing greenhouse gas emissions.
Skea said uncertainty over the schedule was making it difficult for volunteer scientists to plan their work alongside professional and personal commitments. Researchers still do not know what will be expected of them in early 2027, he added.
Governments will have another opportunity to resolve the dispute when the IPCC resumes its suspended plenary session on December 1. The meeting is expected to address the assessment timetable and budget for 2027 and beyond.
“Climate action without climate science is like a ship without a rudder,” Skea told delegates, stressing that scientific evidence must remain central to global climate policy.
The IPCC’s assessment reports provide governments with scientific evidence to guide climate policies, emissions targets and adaptation strategies, as well as international negotiations under the Paris Agreement.
Despite the uncertainty, Skea urged countries not to delay stronger climate action while waiting for the next assessments, saying existing scientific findings could support stronger commitments and faster implementation.
The three reports are at different stages of preparation. The physical science assessment is being revised before government and expert review. The expert review of the impacts and adaptation report is scheduled to close on December 4, while review of the emissions reduction report is due to begin on November 16.
The IPCC also plans to publish three reports in 2027. These include a special report on climate change and cities, scheduled for an approval session in March, and two reports setting out methodologies for governments to report greenhouse gas emissions and removals under the UN climate convention.
The methodologies are intended to improve the consistency, transparency and comparability of national emissions reporting.
For climate-vulnerable countries such as Bangladesh, timely assessments are important for understanding future risks, strengthening adaptation plans and informing development decisions.
The December 1 plenary will be a key test of whether governments can overcome their differences and keep the Seventh Assessment Report on schedule.

item.title: Iran says two oil tankers on fire in Hormuz
item.description:
Iran’s Revolutionary Guards said Tuesday that two oil tankers were on fire in the Strait of Hormuz, where the country regularly targets ships that transit without its authorization.
Since the outbreak of the Middle East war in late February, Tehran has heavily restricted traffic through the strategic waterway, insisting vessels use routes authorized by the Islamic Republic.
The United States has in response imposed a naval blockade on Iranian ports and helped tankers travel the strait, which normally carries about one-fifth of global oil.
“Two violating oil tankers, travelling along an unauthorized route in the Strait of Hormuz, have been brought to a halt following massive explosions and are left burning,” the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, the ideological arm of Iran’s military, said in a statement.
The Guards did not specify the names or origins of the tankers.
Tehran has made multiple announcements in recent weeks saying ships had caught fire in the strait.
It has said some vessels struck mines, but the US military recently claimed all mines had been cleared from the waterway.
US Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the region, also said last month that it had helped Gulf countries export 1.5 billion barrels of oil via Hormuz since the summer.
On Tuesday, the Guards said “one of the vessels -- a super tanker -- struck a naval mine, resulting in an explosion.”
“The second tanker, which was under the escort of the aggressor American military and attempting a covert passage via an illegal route, also had an incident,” they added.

item.title: US calls for ‘new’ Europe security framework as Russia-Ukraine talks open
item.description:
US-mediated talks between Russia and Ukraine on ending more than four years of war opened in Abu Dhabi Tuesday, with Washington calling for a “new” security framework, as Europe fears US President Donald Trump plans a deal with Moscow on the continent’s future.
Russian and Ukrainian negotiators sat facing each other, with Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner and business partner Steve Witkoff at the head of the table.
Kyiv’s delegation -- headed by intelligence chief Rustem Umerov -- met the US envoys as well as European and Nato officials ahead of negotiations.
Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine has killed hundreds of thousands. As another winter of war approaches, Ukraine and its European allies fear Washington will force Kyiv to accept a de facto defeat.
Trump has also floated a deal with Russia on rewriting Europe’s post-war security.
As the talks opened, Kushner said the US hoped to “create the right security relationships between Ukraine and Russia and Europe so that not only we end this war, we create a new framework and a new understanding” that will secure “decades, if not centuries, of peace.”
He conceded there was a “lot of intense emotions” in Ukraine, Russia and Europe.
Before launching its 2022 invasion, Moscow had demanded that Nato roll back troops from eastern Europe and has throughout the war aired its grievances towards the West.
Russia has, for the first time, included in its delegation a diplomat -- Sergei Ryabkov -- who issued an ultimatum to the West on re-writing European security before Moscow launched the war.
The head of Moscow’s delegation, President Vladimir Putin’s nationalistic aide Vladimir Medinsky, said he hoped Moscow’s “bigger and more professional” team will “enable us to move forwards on the path towards peace.”
A source in the Russian team earlier said that “the Ukrainian settlement, whilst a critically important issue, is merely one item on the agenda” of the talks.
The main objective was “the creation of a comprehensive and indivisible security architecture for the entire continent,” it added.
Nato’s general in Europe, Alexus Grynkewich, is also taking part in the talks.
In a joint statement, the Europeans, Ukraine, US and Nato said they held a meeting before meeting Russia, reaffirming their “shared commitment to a strong post-war European security architecture.”
Europe has been alarmed by Trump’s plans and the EU said on the eve of the talks that “meaningful” security discussions can only take place after a ceasefire in Ukraine.
Putin has refused broader ceasefires and face-to-face talks with Ukraine’s Volodymyr Zelensky, vowing his troops will press on to seize more land in Ukraine.
Kyiv’s top negotiator Umerov said Ukraine’s priority in the talks remained securing a ceasefire.
“Our people are waiting to end this war,” he said.
Ukraine has resisted Russia’s invasion at a huge human cost, with thousands of civilians killed and millions forced to flee their homes.
“We hope that we will achieve a lasting peace for Ukraine,” Umerov said, saying Kyiv wanted to discuss “security guarantees.”
There is huge distrust in Ukraine towards Trump’s aims, with the US leader appearing to veer towards Moscow this year, signing a diesel deal with Putin and criticizing Zelensky.
Trump hinted ahead of the talks that Ukraine might have to give up land, saying: “They’re going to end up with a little bit different shape, Ukraine.”
Russia occupies large swathes of Ukraine but, while its troops have inched westwards, they have not been able to seize the whole of the Donetsk region.
Moscow demands Kyiv surrender the parts of the region it still controls, vowing it will otherwise press on with its offensive.
Russia pummeled Ukraine in the run-up to the talks and carried out one of its deadliest strikes yet -- with Kyiv saying 55 people were killed in a frontline village as they queued for humanitarian aid.
Zelensky said the intensified strikes were part of Moscow’s strategy of “putting pressure on Ukraine’s position” at the negotiations.
The Ukrainian military said on Tuesday that Russia had fired 162 drones and one ballistic missile overnight.
Kushner and Witkoff are bringing the enemy sides together for the first time since February, when negotiations took place in Geneva.
Russia and Ukraine have held several rounds of failed talks during almost five years of war and hopes for peace are low.
“We don’t have any particular expectations,” a senior Ukrainian official in Kyiv told AFP.
